title: Fuentes v. Shevin (1972)
summary: Statutes letting a private creditor obtain a writ of replevin and have officers seize household goods on a conclusory application and a bond, without a prior hearing, deny due process: a temporary deprivation counts, a buyer’s possessory interest under a conditional sales contract is property, necessities are not the limit, and only truly extraordinary situations justify seizure before a hearing.
notes:
Mitchell and North Georgia Finishing refine the significance of prior judicial scrutiny, an existing creditor interest, and prompt procedures to dissolve an attachment. Do not read Fuentes as eliminating every prejudgment remedy.

Margarita Fuentes bought a gas stove and a stereo from Firestone on conditional sales contracts; after a dispute over servicing she stopped paying with about $200 left, and a sheriff seized the goods on a writ obtained from a court clerk on a double-value bond before she had even received the summons.

Justice Stewart wrote for a 4–3 Court; Justice White dissented, joined by Chief Justice Burger and Justice Blackmun; Justices Powell and Rehnquist did not participate.

sections.Parties: Margarita Fuentes, a Florida consumer whose household goods were seized, was the appellant; Robert Shevin, Florida’s Attorney General, defended the statute, and Firestone Tire and Rubber Company, the seller, was also an appellee. In the companion Pennsylvania case, Parham v. Cortese, consumers whose goods had been seized under Pennsylvania’s replevin statute sued state officials and creditors. The consumers sought declarations that the statutes were unconstitutional and injunctions against their enforcement.
sections.Material Facts: Fuentes bought a gas stove and later a stereophonic phonograph from Firestone under conditional sales contracts, about $500 plus more than $100 in financing; Firestone kept title but she was entitled to possession unless she defaulted. After more than a year of payments, with about $200 left, a dispute arose over servicing the stove and Firestone sued in small-claims court for repossession. Before she received the summons Firestone obtained a writ of replevin, and a deputy sheriff and a Firestone agent seized the stove and stereo from her home. Florida let the writ issue on a conclusory allegation of entitlement and a bond for double the goods’ value; the clerk issued it, and the defendant had three days to post a counterbond. Pennsylvania was more summary still: an affidavit of value and a bond, no suit required, and the person seized against had to sue to get a hearing.
sections.Procedural History: Fuentes sued in federal district court challenging Florida’s prejudgment replevin procedure under the Due Process Clause, and the Pennsylvania appellants brought a similar suit. In each a three-judge district court, then required for suits to enjoin state statutes as unconstitutional, upheld the statute: Fuentes v. Faircloth, 317 F. Supp. 954 (S.D. Fla. 1970), and Epps v. Cortese, 326 F. Supp. 127 (E.D. Pa. 1971). The consumers appealed directly to the Supreme Court, which vacated and remanded on June 12, 1972. Justice Stewart wrote for four Justices (Douglas, Brennan, Marshall); Justice White dissented, joined by Chief Justice Burger and Justice Blackmun; Justices Powell and Rehnquist, who joined the Court after argument, took no part.
sections.Issue: Do statutes that allow a private party to obtain a writ of replevin and have state officers seize goods from another person’s possession, on an ex parte application and a bond, without notice or an opportunity for a hearing before the seizure, violate the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment?
sections.Holding: Yes. The Florida and Pennsylvania statutes were unconstitutional insofar as they denied the right to an opportunity to be heard before chattels are taken from their possessor. To serve its purpose the hearing must come when the deprivation can still be prevented. A temporary, nonfinal deprivation is a deprivation; a buyer’s possessory interest in goods bought under a conditional sales contract is property even though the seller retains title; and due process protects property generally, not only necessities. Seizure without a prior hearing is permitted only in extraordinary situations, absent where only private gain was at stake. The printed clauses permitting the seller to retake the goods did not waive the right to a prior hearing.
sections.Reasoning: When the defendant received the complaint her goods had already been seized on a private party’s say-so, with no state official deciding whether to issue the writ or weighing the need for immediate seizure; the State acted largely in the dark. The right to be heard protects use and possession against arbitrary encroachment and minimizes mistaken deprivations, so it must be honored when the deprivation can still be prevented. Three limiting arguments failed: a counterbond within three days did not make the seizure a non-deprivation, because a temporary deprivation is a deprivation; the buyers’ possessory interest, dearly bought by installments, was property although the sellers held title; and the Fourteenth Amendment speaks of property generally, so courts should not rank which consumer goods deserve protection. Seizure before a hearing is permitted only in truly unusual situations where an important public interest requires very prompt action and a government official decides under a narrowly drawn statute; private gain is not such an interest. Contract language that the seller “may retake” the goods said nothing about waiving a hearing; a waiver of constitutional rights must at least be clear.

sources.label: Brief · Notice, service and hearing briefs, pp. 27–29

learning.why: The challenged replevin procedures could not authorize seizure of disputed household goods solely on a private creditor’s application without an adequate prior opportunity to be heard.

topics.cp-prejudgment: A temporary loss of possession before judgment was itself a deprivation requiring procedural justification.
topics.cp-hearing: A creditor’s application and bond did not replace an opportunity to contest seizure under the challenged procedures.
topics.cp-waiver: The contractual language did not establish a sufficiently clear waiver of the procedural protection.
topics.cp-due-process: Fuentes is the foundational statement that a prior hearing is normally required before a temporary deprivation of a possessory property interest.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice White, joined by Chief Justice Burger and Justice Blackmun, dissented: the creditor also has a property interest in installment goods that can be hidden, damaged or depreciate while the defaulting debtor keeps them, defaults are rarely disputed so a prior hearing adds cost and delay for little benefit, and creditors can avoid the decision by adding a hearing waiver to their forms, making the result “no more than ideological tinkering with state law.” Two years later Mitchell v. W.T. Grant upheld Louisiana’s sequestration procedure, and Justice Stewart, dissenting there, said Fuentes had effectively been overruled.
